modules.title: Name the whole
modules.desc: Read a fraction as EQUAL parts of a named whole; the denominator counts the equal parts.
modules.rule: A fraction a/b means: cut the whole into b EQUAL parts, then take a of them.
teach: The denominator is the number of equal parts the whole is cut into.
The numerator is how many of those equal parts we keep.
If the parts are not equal, the picture does not show a fraction yet.
contrast: Unequal parts do NOT make a fraction
modules.transfer: You will reuse 'name the whole' in every later module — percentages too.

modules.title: Part and its complement
modules.desc: From a figure, read shaded vs unshaded; a part and its complement add to the whole.
teach: Count the shaded parts, then the unshaded parts — together they make the whole.
If the question asks for UNSHADED, do not give the shaded count by mistake.
The two fractions always add to 1.
modules.transfer: This 'part + complement' idea becomes 'percent + its complement' later.

modules.title: Equivalent fractions
modules.desc: Make equal fractions by multiplying or dividing numerator AND denominator by the same number.
modules.rule: a/b = (a x k)/(b x k): multiply BOTH by the same k (never add).
teach: Multiplying top and bottom by the same number keeps the value the same.
You are really multiplying by k/k = 1.
Adding the same number to top and bottom changes the value — that is the trap.
contrast: x same number: value stays equal
modules.transfer: Equivalent fractions let you build common denominators later.

modules.title: Lowest terms
modules.desc: Reduce a fraction fully by dividing numerator and denominator by their greatest common divisor.
modules.rule: Divide top and bottom by their GCD once to reach lowest terms.
teach: The GCD is the biggest number that divides BOTH top and bottom.
Divide both by the GCD in one clean step to reach lowest terms.
Do not flip the fraction or stop after a partial reduction.
contrast: Partial reduction leaves a common factor behind
modules.transfer: Lowest-terms answers are the standard form your mock tests expect.

modules.title: Compare fractions
modules.desc: Decide which fraction is greater using a common denominator or cross-multiplying.
modules.rule: Compare a/b and c/d by comparing a x d with c x b (cross products).
teach: A bigger bottom number does NOT mean a bigger fraction.
Give both fractions the same denominator, then compare the tops.
Or cross-multiply: a x d versus c x b.
modules.transfer: Comparing by common denominator leads straight into adding unlike fractions.

modules.title: Add and subtract like fractions
modules.desc: Add or subtract fractions with the SAME denominator by working only on the numerators.
modules.rule: a/d ± b/d = (a ± b)/d — keep the denominator, combine the tops.
teach: Same-size pieces add by counting: 3 eighths + 2 eighths = 5 eighths.
The denominator stays the same — you are not making new piece sizes.
Adding the denominators is the trap; the piece size does not change.
modules.transfer: Once bottoms match, adding is easy — that is why unlike fractions get a common bottom first.

modules.title: Add and subtract unlike fractions
modules.desc: Give unlike fractions a common denominator (the LCM), then combine the numerators.
modules.rule: Rewrite both over the LCM of the bottoms, then add/subtract the tops.
teach: Different-size pieces cannot be counted together until they match.
Use the LCM of the bottoms as the common denominator.
Adding across without a common bottom (top+top over bottom+bottom) is the trap.
modules.transfer: This is the heart of fraction arithmetic in equations and word problems.

modules.title: Mixed and improper fractions
modules.desc: Convert between a mixed number and an improper fraction using whole x denominator + numerator.
modules.rule: w n/d = (w x d + n)/d; reverse by dividing to get whole and remainder.
teach: To go to improper: multiply the whole by the denominator, then add the numerator.
To go to mixed: divide the top by the bottom — quotient is the whole, remainder is the new top.
Adding the whole straight onto the numerator is the trap.
contrast: whole x denom + num = new top
modules.transfer: Improper form makes multiplying and dividing mixed numbers simple.

modules.title: A fraction of a quantity
modules.desc: Find a fraction OF a number: divide by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator.
modules.rule: a/b of N = (N ÷ b) x a — share into b, take a shares.
teach: 'of' means multiply: a/b of N = a/b x N.
Divide N by the denominator to find one share, then take 'numerator' shares.
Dividing by the numerator only (ignoring the denominator) is the trap.
contrast: x by numerator = how many shares
modules.transfer: Fraction-of-a-quantity is exactly how percentages of amounts work.

modules.title: Fraction equations and word problems
modules.desc: Solve missing-number fraction equations and word problems by working back from the whole.
modules.rule: Name the whole, write the fraction relationship, then solve for the unknown.
teach: In 'remaining = whole - known fractions', the leftover count pins down the whole.
For like-fraction equations, scale the single term up to the target.
For numerator-defined-by-denominator problems, build the numerator from the rule first.
contrast: Find the WHOLE from the leftover
Then take the asked fraction of it
modules.transfer: This is the reasoning IPM word problems reward most.

questions.title: Build to twelfths
questions.story: Write a fraction equal to 3/4 that has 12 on the bottom.

stages.prompt: To turn the bottom 4 into 12, what do you do?
stages.hint: Find the number that 4 is multiplied by to reach 12.

options.feedback: Yes — 4 x 3 = 12, so the multiplier is 3.
Adding changes the value. Equivalent fractions come from MULTIPLYING.
That would make the bottom 48, far too big. Use the factor 3.

stages.prompt: What must you do to the TOP to keep the fraction equal?
stages.hint: Whatever you do to the bottom, do the SAME to the top.

options.feedback: Right — multiply top and bottom by the same 3; that is multiplying by 3/3 = 1.
Changing only the bottom changes the value — the fraction would no longer be equal.
Mixing 'multiply bottom, add top' breaks the equality. Multiply BOTH.

stages.prompt: Which fraction is equal to the original?
stages.hint: Compute 3 x 3 over 4 x 3.

options.feedback: Yes — 3 x 3 = 9 and 4 x 3 = 12, giving 9/12.
This came from ADDING 3 to each — 6/7 is not equal to 3/4.
Only the top was multiplied here; the bottom must change too.

worked: Multiply the top by the same 3: 3 x 3 = 9.

options.feedback: Right — one 6th of 54 is 54 ÷ 6 = 9.
That divided by the NUMERATOR; one share comes from dividing by the denominator.
Finding a share is division into equal parts, not subtraction.

stages.prompt: How many of those shares do we take?
stages.hint: Take the numerator, 5, of the shares.

options.feedback: Yes — the numerator 5 tells how many 6ths to take.
Taking all 6 shares would give back the whole 54; take just 5.
One share is only 9; the numerator 5 says take 5 of them.

stages.prompt: So how many are in the asked part?
stages.hint: Multiply one share by 5.

options.feedback: Yes — 9 x 5 = 45 beads.
This used the share from dividing by the numerator, so it misses the real count.
That is ALL the beads; only 5/6 of them are asked for.

questions.check: Asked part 45 + rest 9 = 54 beads in all.

questions.title: Library, lab, playground
questions.story: In a class, 3/7 of the students went to the library and 2/7 went to the science lab. The remaining 14 students went to the playground. How many went to the library?

stages.prompt: What fraction of the class went to the playground?
stages.hint: The three groups together make the whole (7/7).

options.feedback: Right — 3/7 + 2/7 = 5/7 left, so 2/7 remain for the playground.
5/7 is the part that went to library and lab TOGETHER, not the remainder.
Subtract both known fractions from 7/7: 7/7 - 3/7 - 2/7 = 2/7, not 1/7.

stages.prompt: 14 students are 2/7 of the class. What is the WHOLE class?
stages.hint: If 2/7 is 14, one 7th is 14 ÷ 2.

options.feedback: Yes — one 7th is 14 ÷ 2 = 7, so the whole is 7 x 7 = 49.
That doubled the remainder; instead find one 7th first, then scale to 7 sevenths.
14 is TWO sevenths, not one, so multiply one 7th (which is 7) by 7, giving 49.

stages.prompt: How many went to the library (3/7 of 49)?
stages.hint: One 7th is 7; take 3 of them.

options.feedback: Yes — 3/7 of 49 is 3 x 7 = 21 students.
14 is the playground group (2/7), not the library group (3/7).
7 is just one 7th; the library share is 3 sevenths, so 3 x 7 = 21.

worked: 2/7 of the class = 14, so one 7th = 7 and the whole = 49.
questions.explain: Why does the leftover count tell us the size of the whole class?

questions.title: Filling the water tank

stages.prompt: What fraction of the tank is still EMPTY?

options.feedback: Right — 4/7 is full, so 3/7 is still empty.
4/7 is the FILLED part; the empty part is what the 120 litres will fill.

stages.prompt: 120 litres fill the empty 3/7. How big is one 7th?

options.feedback: Yes — 3 sevenths hold 120 litres, so one 7th is 40 litres.
That multiplied instead of dividing; one of the 3 sevenths is 120 ÷ 3 = 40.
120 litres fill THREE sevenths together, so one 7th is smaller.

stages.prompt: What is the TOTAL capacity (7 sevenths)?
stages.hint: Multiply one 7th by 7.

options.feedback: Yes — 7 x 40 = 280 litres total capacity.
That is only the filled 4/7; the whole tank is all 7 sevenths.
Recount: one 7th is 40, and 7 x 40 = 280, not 240.

questions.explain: Why does the 'litres needed' describe the EMPTY fraction, not the full one?

questions.explain: Why is the balance the COMPLEMENT (2/5), not the withdrawn 3/5?

questions.title: The repeated numerator
questions.story: The same number fills every box: box/7 + box/7 + box/7 + box/7 = 48/28. What number is the box?

stages.prompt: Simplify the right side, 48/28, to lowest terms.
stages.hint: Divide top and bottom by their GCD.

options.feedback: Right — the GCD of 48 and 28 is 4, giving 12/7.
That only divided by 2 — keep going: 24/14 = 12/7 in lowest terms.
Both 48 and 28 are even, so it can still be reduced to 12/7.

stages.prompt: Add the four like fractions on the left. What do you get?
stages.hint: Same bottom 7, so add the tops: box four times.

options.feedback: Yes — four copies of box/7 is (4 x box)/7.
Adding like fractions keeps the bottom 7; it does not become 7 x 4 = 28 on top of one box.
All four terms count; together they make (4 x box)/7.

stages.prompt: Solve (4 x box)/7 = 12/7. What is box?
stages.hint: Same bottom, so 4 x box = 12.

options.feedback: Yes — 4 x box = 12, so box = 3.
12 is 4 x box, not box itself; divide by 4 to get 3.
48 was before simplifying; after reducing, 4 x box = 12, so box = 3.

questions.explain: Why can we compare only the tops once both sides share the denominator 7?

questions.title: Numerator tells the denominator
questions.story: The numerator of a fraction is 21. The denominator is 16 less than the numerator. Write the fraction as a mixed number.

stages.prompt: What is the denominator?
stages.hint: Denominator = numerator - 16.

options.feedback: Right — 16 less than 21 is 21 - 16 = 5.
16 is the amount you subtract, not the denominator itself.
'16 less than' means subtract 16, not add it.

stages.prompt: So the fraction is 21/5. Is it proper or improper?
stages.hint: Compare the top with the bottom.

options.feedback: Yes — the top is larger than the bottom, so 21/5 is improper and makes a mixed number.
Not always; when the top exceeds the bottom the fraction is more than 1.
21 ÷ 5 is 4 with a remainder, so it is 4 and a bit, not exactly 4.

stages.prompt: Convert 21/5 to a mixed number:
stages.hint: 21 ÷ 5 = whole remainder.

options.feedback: Yes — 5 goes into 21 four times with 1 left over, so 4 1/5.
16 was only the difference; the denominator is 5, so the leftover is over 5.
That is 9/5, far too small; 21/5 is 4 1/5.

questions.explain: Why does 'the denominator is 16 less than the numerator' set the bottom, not the leftover?

questions.title: Find the missing numerator
questions.story: Find the number for the box: 6 + box/8 = 7 3/8.

stages.prompt: Subtract 6 from both sides. What must box/8 equal?
stages.hint: 7 3/8 - 6 leaves the fractional part plus one whole.

options.feedback: That dropped the extra whole; 7 3/8 - 6 is 1 3/8, not just 3/8.
7 3/8 - 6 = 1 3/8 exactly; recheck the whole-number part.

stages.prompt: Write 1 3/8 as an improper fraction over 8.
stages.hint: 1 whole = 8/8.

options.feedback: You cannot add the whole straight onto the numerator; 1 = 8/8 first.
That ignored the whole number 1; include 8/8 as well.

stages.prompt: So box/8 = 11/8. What is box?
stages.hint: Same bottom means the tops match.

options.feedback: Yes — equal bottoms, so box = 11.
8 is the denominator, not the numerator we are solving for.
3 is only the leftover eighths; the whole adds 8 more, giving 11.

questions.explain: Why must we turn the whole number into eighths before reading the numerator?

That doubled the remainder; the whole is far bigger — 135 plants.

stages.prompt: How many are sunflowers AND marigolds (1/9 + 4/9 of 135)?
stages.hint: That is 5/9 of 135; one 9th is 15.

30 is the hibiscus group; sunflowers + marigolds are 5 ninths, giving 75.
One 9th is 15; together sunflowers and marigolds are 5 ninths, so 75.

worked: 2/9 = 30, so one 9th = 15 and the whole = 9 x 15 = 135.
questions.explain: Why does the hibiscus remainder unlock the size of the whole garden?
